question: What is the main problem in the body that causes diabetes mellitus?

options.A: Defects in insulin production or action

explanation: Think of diabetes as a trouble with insulin—either the body isn't making enough of it, or it's not using the insulin it has properly, which leaves too much sugar in the blood. You've got this! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h1)

question: Over time, why does high blood sugar cause damage to organs?

options.A: Sugar molecules directly injure delicate blood vessels and nerves
options.B: Glucose turns into a toxic acid inside major body organs
options.C: The pancreas stops producing all red blood cells
options.D: Extra sugar blocks the normal flow of oxygen to the lungs

explanation: When blood sugar stays high for too long, it acts almost like sandpaper on the tiny, delicate blood vessels and nerves all over the body. Spotting this early helps us protect our patients! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h1)

question: Why do patients with untreated diabetes always feel very thirsty and pee a lot?

options.A: Excess blood sugar pulls large amounts of water into the urine as the kidneys filter it out
options.B: Dehydration is caused by a simultaneous infection in the bladder
options.C: The liver stores extra water to dilute circulating blood sugar
options.D: High insulin levels trick the brain into thinking the body is dehydrated

explanation: When the kidneys try to wash away all that extra sugar, water naturally follows it out. That leads to heavy urination and leaves the patient feeling super thirsty. Makes total sense when you picture it! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h2)

question: What is the main job of insulin at the cellular level?

options.A: It converts dietary protein directly into red blood cells
options.B: It signals the kidneys to absorb more sugar into the bloodstream
options.C: It destroys excess bacteria circulating in the plasma
options.D: It acts as a key to unlock cell receptors and let glucose inside

explanation: You can picture insulin as a tiny key. It unlocks the doors of our body cells so glucose from the food we eat can go inside and give us energy. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h2)

question: What is the main cause of Type 1 diabetes?

options.A: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells
options.B: Gradual resistance of body cells to normal insulin
options.D: Poor dietary intake of refined carbohydrates

explanation: In Type 1 diabetes, the body's immune system gets confused and mistakenly attacks the insulin-making beta cells in the pancreas. Brilliant to keep this distinction in mind! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h3)

question: How is Type 2 diabetes different from Type 1?

options.A: Type 1 can be cured entirely with proper diet and oral medication
options.B: Type 2 only affects elderly individuals who consume high amounts of sugar
options.C: Type 2 involves insulin resistance and relative deficiency rather than complete beta cell destruction
options.D: Type 1 is caused by lifestyle factors while Type 2 is strictly genetic

explanation: In Type 2, the body still makes insulin, but the cells just don't respond to it well (resistance), and the pancreas can't keep up with the extra demand. You're mastering the basics! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h3)

question: A 45-year-old Nigerian civil servant works a desk job and has central obesity. Which condition is he most at risk for?
explanation: Sitting for long hours, lack of exercise, and belly fat are classic risk factors for Type 2 diabetes. Seeing how this connects to real life makes clinical rotations much easier! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h4)

question: Which lifestyle change is a major reason diabetes is becoming more common in Nigerian cities?

options.A: Engaging in heavy manual farm labor every morning
options.B: Consuming excessive amounts of natural spring water
options.C: Increasing daily intake of green leafy vegetables
options.D: Adopting processed diets and reducing physical activity

explanation: With busy city life, more people eat fast, processed foods and move around less. This shift in lifestyle greatly increases metabolic risks. Great insight for community nursing! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h4)

question: What HbA1c blood test result is generally used to diagnose diabetes?
explanation: An HbA1c of 6.5% or higher shows that blood sugar has been running high over the past three months. It's a key lab value you'll use all the time in practice! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h5)

question: What do the three classic signs of diabetes—polyuria, polydipsia, and polyphagia—actually mean?

options.A: Frequent headaches, blurred vision, and dizziness
options.B: High blood pressure, rapid heart rate, and fever
options.C: Joint pain, muscle weakness, and skin rashes
options.D: Excessive urination, excessive thirst, and excessive hunger

explanation: Just break down the medical terms: 'uria' relates to urine, 'dipsia' to thirst, and 'phagia' to eating/hunger! Remembering the Greek roots makes nursing terms so much easier. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h5)

question: What is the main lifelong treatment needed for someone with Type 1 diabetes?
explanation: Since the body isn't making insulin at all in Type 1, patients must take insulin every day to survive. You're doing great with your pharmacology basics! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h6)

question: A patient with diabetes looks shaky, dizzy, and is sweating before lunch. What should the nurse do right away?

options.A: Administer the scheduled dose of daily long-acting insulin
options.B: Send a blood sample to the laboratory for an HbA1c test
options.C: Encourage the patient to sleep until the symptoms pass
options.D: Check blood glucose levels and prepare a fast-acting carbohydrate

explanation: Shakiness and sweating are red flags for low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). Always check the blood glucose first and have a fast sugar source ready! Patient safety comes first. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h6)

question: Why are community health screening programs so important for managing diabetes in Nigeria?

options.A: Many individuals have undiagnosed diabetes and only discover it when complications arise
options.B: Community outreach prevents all forms of genetic Type 1 diabetes
options.C: Public testing eliminates the need for personal blood glucose meters
options.D: Screening programs replace the need for prescription medications entirely

explanation: Lots of people walk around with high blood sugar without knowing it. Community screenings help catch it early before severe damage happens. That's true public health nursing! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h7)

question: Which of these is NOT a main focus of community-level diabetes education?

options.A: Dispelling cultural myths about the causes of chronic illness
options.B: Teaching healthy food substitutions using local ingredients
options.C: Promoting expensive surgical weight-loss procedures for all citizens
options.D: Encouraging affordable physical activity like brisk walking

explanation: Community education focuses on practical, low-cost steps like eating local healthy foods and walking. Expensive surgeries are definitely not standard community advice! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h7)

question: What is the main difference between microvascular and macrovascular complications in diabetes?

options.A: Microvascular conditions involve low blood sugar, while macrovascular conditions involve high blood sugar
options.B: Macrovascular damage is reversible with diet, whereas microvascular damage requires surgery
options.C: Microvascular affects tiny vessels in the eyes, kidneys, and nerves, while macrovascular affects large vessels like the heart and brain
options.D: Microvascular complications only occur in Type 1 while macrovascular only occur in Type 2

explanation: 'Micro' means tiny (eyes, kidneys, nerves), and 'macro' means large (heart, brain). Long-term high sugar hurts both sizes of blood vessels in different ways! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h8)

question: Which acute complication is caused by severe lack of insulin, leading to acid buildup and ketones in Type 1 diabetes?
explanation: When cells can't get glucose without insulin, the body burns fat instead. This process makes acidic byproducts called ketones, causing diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). You're tackling advanced concepts like a pro! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h8)
